title: Before you begin: have something to say
body:
Read and annotate before polishing an opening. Write a rough answer to the guiding question and identify two or three details that could support it. If you can only list techniques, return to the text: what do those choices help it communicate?

You can draft the thesis first, then write the introductory sentences that lead into it.

title: Step 1 — Identify the text and its immediate situation
body:
Give the reader the essentials: the creator, title and text type where supplied, and what is happening or being addressed. Include contextual information only when it helps explain your reading.

- **Literature:** establish the situation, speaker or narrative perspective that matters. Distinguish author from narrator or speaker. You do not need to invent a target demographic or reduce a poem to a single persuasive purpose.
- **Language & Literature:** identify the communication situation and a plausible audience and purpose, supported by the text. Publication details can help, but do not guess a date or background story.

**Check:** Could someone locate your analysis in this particular text, rather than any poem, speech or advertisement?

title: Step 2 — Move from subject to interpretation
body:
The subject names what the text is about. Your interpretation explains what it makes of that subject.

“An advertisement about smoking” identifies a subject. “An advertisement that presents smoking as a loss of independence” makes a claim that can be examined through its choices.

Ask yourself:

- What tension, change, attitude or relationship becomes significant?
- How does the text shape our understanding of its subject?
- What is less obvious than the literal events or stated message?

Keep the claim proportionate to the evidence. A precise, qualified interpretation is stronger than an impressive-sounding claim you cannot support.

title: Step 3 — Answer the guiding question
body:
Turn your interpretation towards the analytical focus of the question. If it asks about the relationship between words and images, your thesis needs to explain that relationship—not merely say both are present.

A useful thesis connects **the relevant choices or pattern** with **the meaning they create**. It need not list three devices, fit into one sentence, or begin with a memorised phrase.

**Thin claim:** “The advertisement uses imagery, language and layout to persuade the reader.”

**More specific claim:** “By making attachment to cigarettes visible as dependence on oxygen equipment, the advertisement presents smoking as a threat to independence.”

The second claim gives the essay something to demonstrate. It remains a reading to test, not a substitute for the analysis that follows.

title: Step 4 — Give the response a direction
body:
Let the thesis suggest the ideas the body will develop. You might trace a shift, explore a tension, or examine how different choices work together.

Avoid promising a tour of devices: “First I will discuss imagery, then diction, then structure.” Organise around what you want to establish about the text. Mention a technique when it clarifies that argument.

You do not need an additional roadmap sentence if your thesis already makes the direction clear.

title: Step 5 — Join the sentences and remove the scaffolding
Final self-check
body:
- Have I identified the text using reliable information?
- Have I established more than its general topic?
- Does my thesis answer the guiding question?
- Can I point to details that support each main claim?
- Does the introduction lead naturally into my first analytical paragraph?

title: Practice: revise one move
body: Underline the sentence that answers the guiding question. If you cannot find one, write it before adding anything else. Then circle any sentence that could introduce almost any text. Make it specific or remove it.
